nameStory: The 'moondust' in this lichen's name comes from the fine, powdery white specks scattered across its surface, which sparkle like cosmic dust in the right light. These tiny granules, called soredia, help the lichen reproduce and give it an otherworldly, celestial appearance that's unmistakable once you know what to look for.
description: Moondust Speckled Lichen is a leafy, foliose lichen that forms spreading patches on tree bark throughout New England. It has a grayish-green color with distinctive white, powdery spots scattered across its surface like fine dust. The lichen grows in overlapping, leaf-like lobes that can spread several inches across. It's part of the shield lichen family, known for their flat, shield-like growth pattern against tree bark.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Look for fine white powdery granules (soredia) scattered across the surface like moondust - you can gently brush these with your finger and they'll feel slightly gritty

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms flat, leaf-like lobes that overlap like shingles, growing tightly pressed against tree bark with slightly raised edges

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Grayish-green when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet from rain or morning dew

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Grows exclusively on tree bark, favoring both hardwoods like oak and maple, as well as conifers

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual patches can spread 3-6 inches across, with lobes typically 1/4 to 1/2 inch wide

habitat: You'll find Moondust Speckled Lichen on the bark of both hardwood and conifer trees throughout New England's forests. It's particularly common on oak, maple, pine, and fir trees in mixed woodlands from sea level up to mid-elevations. Look for it in mature forests where the air quality is relatively good, as lichens are sensitive to pollution.

seasonality.spring: More vibrant green coloration appears as spring rains wet the lichen. The white soredia become more noticeable against the fresh green background.
seasonality.summer: During dry spells, the lichen appears more grayish and subdued. Hot, humid days can bring out the green tones even without rain.
seasonality.fall: Often looks its most dramatic as autumn moisture enhances the green color, creating beautiful contrast against colorful fall foliage on host trees.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible and identifiable under snow. The white soredia can be particularly striking against dark, wet bark during winter thaws.

funFact: This lichen can live for decades or even centuries on the same tree - some specimens are older than the oldest human residents of New England, slowly growing outward at just a few millimeters per year like a living geological formation.
confusionNotes: It's easily confused with its close relatives like Eastern Speckled Shield Lichen and Rough Speckled Shield Lichen, which also have white soredia. The key difference is in the arrangement and texture of the white granules - Moondust has finer, more evenly scattered soredia that truly look like cosmic dust rather than chunky white patches.
contextualKnowledge: All speckled shield lichens were once grouped together under different scientific names, leading to confusion in older field guides. The genus Punctelia was separated out relatively recently, so you might find this species listed under the old name Parmelia in vintage nature books.
compareHints: Compared to other Punctelia species in New England, Moondust Speckled Lichen has the finest, most evenly distributed white soredia - like someone dusted it with powdered sugar. Rough Speckled Shield Lichen has coarser, more irregular white patches, while Eastern Speckled Shield Lichen tends to have soredia concentrated along the lobe edges rather than scattered across the entire surface.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its speckled shield relatives in New England, rough speckled shield lichen stands out with its light-colored underside and relatively large, broad lobes around the edges.
